tab1.scan_sim_title: 🔍 Row-by-Row RAM Scan Simulation (5 sample rows)
tab1.join_mechanism_note: JOIN Mechanism in SSBM & SIGMOD 2008: lo.orderdate is a Day Index (0..2404). Filtering d_year = 1993 corresponds to orderdate BETWEEN 365 AND 729. Query Q1.1 evaluates entirely on 1 Fact table with predicate: orderdate BETWEEN 365 AND 729 AND discount BETWEEN 1 AND 3 AND quantity < 25.
tab1.cache_point1_desc: Each fact row is a contiguous 68-byte struct. A modern CPU cache line is 64 bytes, causing each row to straddle across 2 cache lines. When the query only accesses 4 columns (orderdate, discount, quantity, revenue - total 16 bytes), the CPU must still fetch the full 68 bytes, wasting 76.5% of memory bus bandwidth and severely polluting L1/L2/L3 caches.
tab1.cache_point2_desc: Each column is stored as an independent, contiguous 1D array in RAM. A single 64-byte cache line packs 16 int32 values (4 bytes each). When scanning the orderdate column, 100% of data loaded into cache is actively utilized (0% waste). Furthermore, this sequential access pattern enables CPU hardware prefetchers to stream upcoming cache lines at near-zero latency.

plan.title: Execution Plans Comparison (SIGMOD 2008)
plan.plan_a_title: Plan A: Traditional Row-Store (Early Materialization + Hash Join)
plan.plan_a_point1: Fact I/O: Reads all 17 Fact attributes (68B/row · 408 MB), consuming 100% table volume.
plan.plan_a_point2: Early Materialization: Joins wide tuples early, passing full 68B structs through 3 hash tables.
plan.plan_a_point3: Intermediate Buffers: Allocates massive temporary buffers in RAM, choking system bus and causing L1/L2 cache thrashing.
plan.plan_a_point4: Empirical Timing: Measured baseline across 6 million rows.
plan.plan_b_title: Plan B: Column-Store + Invisible Join (Hash Table Lookup)
plan.plan_b_point1: Fact I/O: Scans only 3 FK columns (12B/row) + single revenue column at qualified positions (72.9 MB, ~82% I/O reduction).
plan.plan_b_point2: Late Materialization: Postpones attribute retrieval to the final step after Position List P is materialized.
plan.plan_b_point3: Zero Intermediate Tuples: Eliminates intermediate JOIN tuples; join evaluations become vector bitwise AND in CPU Cache.
plan.plan_b_point4: Empirical Timing: Substantially faster than Row-Store.
plan.plan_c_title: Plan C: Column-Store + Invisible Join (Between-Predicate Rewriting)
plan.plan_c_point1: Between-Predicate Rewriting (Section 5.4.2): Identifies contiguous key bounds (lo <= key <= hi) for customer, supplier, orderdate to replace hash lookups with range checks.
plan.plan_c_point2: Bitmap AND & Late Materialization: Intersects 3 FK bitmaps into Position List P, then extracts revenue and reverse-lookups Dimensions.
plan.plan_c_point3: Empirical Timing: Fastest overall due to register-level CPU optimizations and SIMD vectorization.

phase.title: 3 Phases of Invisible Join Principle (SIGMOD 2008)
phase.phase1_desc: The CPU independently evaluates WHERE predicates on small Dimension tables (CUSTOMER, SUPPLIER, DWDATE). Qualified primary keys populate small Hash Sets (ht_c, ht_s, ht_d). Because Dimension tables are tiny, entire Hash Sets fit comfortably inside L1/L2 CPU Cache.
phase.phase2_title: Phase 2: Fact Probing & Bitmap AND (Fact Probing & Vectorized Bitwise AND)
phase.phase2_desc: The CPU independently scans each foreign key column array of Fact (custkey, suppkey, orderdate) and probes Hash Sets to yield Bitmaps. It then executes vectorized bitwise AND across bit arrays to produce Position List P containing qualified row indices.
phase.phase3_title: Phase 3: Late Materialization & GROUP BY (Late Materialization & Aggregation)
phase.phase3_desc: Only for indices in Position List P, the CPU extracts the single revenue column from Fact, while reverse-looking up Dimension tables to fetch nation names and years for GROUP BY. Achieves ~82%–83% Fact I/O savings (~69.4–72.8 MB vs 408 MB for Row-Store, surpassing 76.5% of standard projection) with zero intermediate tuples.

star_schema.title: Star Schema Benchmark (SSBM) Architecture
star_schema.point1_title: 1. Central Fact Table: LINEORDER (6,000,000 rows · 408 MB)
star_schema.point1_desc: Accounts for >95% of total database volume. Contains 17 attributes including foreign keys (custkey, suppkey, orderdate, partkey) and numerical measures (revenue, supplycost, discount). In Column-Store, columns are stored as contiguous independent arrays in RAM/Disk.
star_schema.point2_title: 2. Dimension Tables: Highly Compact & CPU Cache-Optimized
star_schema.customer_desc: CUSTOMER (30,000 rows): Contains c_custkey, c_nation, c_region.
star_schema.supplier_desc: SUPPLIER (2,000 rows): Contains s_suppkey, s_nation, s_region.
star_schema.dwdate_desc: DWDATE (2,555 rows): Contains d_datekey, d_year, d_yearmonth.
star_schema.part_desc: PART (200,000 rows): Contains p_partkey, p_mfgr, p_category.
star_schema.point3_desc: The extreme scale asymmetry (Dimensions have thousands of rows while Fact has millions) is the ideal foundation for Invisible Join to keep Dimension Hash Sets inside CPU L1/L2 Cache, transforming expensive joins into lightning-fast integer array scans.

rle.title: Run-Length Encoding (RLE) & Direct Computation Principles (SIGMOD 2008)
rle.point1_desc: Instead of storing 6,000,000 raw integers for the orderdate column (consuming 24 MB RAM), Run-Length Encoding compresses consecutive runs into triples: (value, start_position, count).
rle.point2_desc: Since Fact data is sorted by order date, 6,000,000 rows condense into exactly 2,405 triples. Memory consumption drops from 24 MB to just tens of kilobytes, fitting entirely within CPU L1 Cache.
rle.point3_desc: Breakthrough of C-Store/Column-Store: The CPU evaluates WHERE orderdate BETWEEN 0 AND 2 directly on compressed triples. Only matching positions are produced as position ranges, completely bypassing 6M row decompression.

rle_numbers.title: Detailed Breakdown of 4 Comparison Metrics (Tab 2: RLE)
rle_numbers.metric1_title: 🎯 1. COUNT Result: Why Are Both Outputs 100% Identical?
rle_numbers.metric1_sql: SELECT COUNT(*) FROM lineorder WHERE orderdate BETWEEN 0 AND 2;
rle_numbers.metric1_uncomp: Sequential Scan (Uncompressed): CPU iterates through every single row (3,000,000 or 6,000,000 rows) evaluating the filter condition. Output count matches qualified orders (e.g. 3,792 orders).
rle_numbers.metric1_rle: RLE Direct (Zero Decompression): Zero iterations over 3 million rows! Since orderdate is compressed into 2,405 triples (day, run_length), the engine locates the 3 matching day clusters (days 0, 1, 2) and directly sums their 3 run_length values: COUNT = run_length[0] + run_length[1] + run_length[2] = 1,264 + 1,264 + 1,264 = 3,792 orders.
rle_numbers.metric1_sci: Scientific Significance: RLE is a lossless compression algorithm. Direct calculation on compressed data preserves 100% accuracy while eliminating all decompression overhead (Zero Decompression).
rle_numbers.metric2_title: 🔍 2. Elements Scanned: 3,000,000 rows vs 3 / 2,405 clusters (1,000,000x Reduction)
rle_numbers.metric2_uncomp: Sequential Scan: CPU iterates over 3,000,000 integer array elements (or 6M rows), performing 3,000,000 branch comparisons.
rle_numbers.metric2_rle: RLE Direct: Uses binary search O(log K) over 2,405 clusters to locate boundary indices, then loops over only 3 matching clusters.
rle_numbers.metric2_eff: Efficiency: Number of elements accessed by CPU drops by exactly 1,000,000 times!
rle_numbers.metric3_title: 💾 3. Scanned Footprint: 12.0 MB vs 19.2 KB (Comfortably Fits in L1 Cache)
rle_numbers.metric3_uncomp: Uncompressed: 3,000,000 rows × 4 bytes = 12.0 MB (or 6M × 4B = 24.0 MB). This far exceeds L1 Cache (32–48 KB/core) and L2 Cache, forcing continuous RAM bus fetches.
rle_numbers.metric3_rle: RLE Direct: The entire compressed orderdate array occupies only 2,405 clusters × 8 bytes ≈ 19.2 KB. This resides completely inside CPU L1 Data Cache, delivering maximum memory throughput (1–2 CPU clock cycles) with zero RAM bus traffic!
rle_numbers.metric4_title: ⚡ 4. Processing Time: ~27.750 ms vs ~0.001 ms (~27,000x Faster)
rle_numbers.metric4_uncomp: Sequential Scan: Memory bandwidth bottlenecked (Memory-bound) with branch penalty across millions of loop iterations, taking 25–45 ms.
rle_numbers.metric4_rle: RLE Direct: Takes mere nanoseconds (~0.001 ms displayed in browser) because CPU executes 3 integer additions directly on CPU registers with data in L1 Cache.
rle_numbers.speech_tip_title: 💡 Defense Speech Tip for this section:
rle_numbers.speech_tip_content: "Esteemed committee members, examine the COUNT result: both methods yield exactly 3,792 orders. However, sequential scan had to traverse 3 million rows and fetch 12 MB from RAM; whereas RLE added just 3 integers within a 19 KB L1 Cache without decompressing a single row. This demonstrates the profound efficiency of the Zero-Decompression principle!"

late_mat.title: Late Materialization Principle (SIGMOD 2008)
late_mat.point1_title: 1. Core Concept: Postpone Tuple Stitching to the Final Step
late_mat.point1_desc: While Row-Store performs Early Materialization by joining all 17 attributes across 6,000,000 rows creating a massive temporary table (~408 MB), Column-Store does NOT decompress string attributes in Phase 1 and 2, POSTPONING data access to the very final step.
late_mat.point2_title: 2. Phase 3 Execution Workflow (Based on Position List P)
late_mat.point2_p_desc: Once Phase 2 filtering completes, producing Position List P (~216,000 qualified rows instead of 6M):
late_mat.point2_read_fact: Fact Access: CPU extracts only 1 column (revenue) at positions in P (with 3 FK columns, totaling ~69.4–72.8 MB, saving ~82%–83% Fact I/O vs 408 MB for Row-Store).
late_mat.point2_lookup_dim: Dimension Lookup: Uses foreign keys (custkey, suppkey, orderdate) to reverse-lookup string attributes (c_nation, s_nation, d_year) for GROUP BY.
late_mat.point3_no_inter: No Intermediate JOIN Tuples: Avoids materializing enormous join tuples in RAM.
late_mat.point3_bus_opt: Bus Bandwidth Optimization: Reduces Fact transfer volume by ~82%–83% (from 408 MB to ~69.4–72.8 MB, surpassing 76.5% savings of basic projection).
late_mat.point3_cache_opt: Cache Locality: Late Materialization maintains compact data within CPU L1/L2 caches.

spec.title: Logical Query Specification vs Physical Execution Engine
spec.point1_title: 1. What is the SQL Code Frame?
spec.point1_desc: This is the canonical Logical Query Specification from the Star Schema Benchmark (SSBM) in the original SIGMOD 2008 paper (Prof. Daniel Abadi, Yale / MIT). It defines the standard business problem and query logic.
spec.point2_title: 2. Does the System Connect to an RDBMS (SQL Server / MySQL)?
spec.point2_desc: ABSOLUTELY NOT. The system does not invoke SQL Server or MySQL. If executed via a black-box RDBMS, queries are evaluated as Row-Stores, preventing micro-level measurement of CPU L1/L2 cache latencies and RAM bus bandwidth.
spec.point3_title: 3. How Does the System Physically Execute?
spec.point3_desc: When you click ▶ Run, the system activates a custom Physical Execution Engine written in Python/NumPy operating directly on 6,000,000-row RAM memory arrays:
spec.point3_row: Row-Store: Loads entire 17-column AoS tuple structs (68B/row), wasting 76% of CPU Cache bandwidth.
spec.point3_col: Column-Store: Loads only accessed columns, computes directly on RLE compressed arrays (Zero Decompression), and joins tables via vectorized bit arrays (Invisible Join).
